Introduction¶

In previous exercises we considered supervised learning, i.e., we were given both input data X and output values Y. We now move on to unsupervised learning where we are only provided input data X. The aim is here to find common patterns in the data such as groups of observations that are similar in some sense.

Part A - Mandatory Exercises¶

Below you will find the mandatory exercises for Week 4 of the course Data Mining and Machine Learning.

Exercise 1 - k-means clustering¶

In this part of the exercise we will investigate k-means clustering. In k-means each of the data points are assigned to the cluster in closest proximity according to some measure of distance between cluster centers and data points. When the distance is given by the squared euclidian distance, the centers are also called centroids. Once the data points have been assigned, each cluster center is updated to be placed at the center of the data points that are assigned to the cluster. This continues iteratively, usually until the assignment of data points to centers no longer changes or until a maximal number of iterations is reached.

Exercise 1.1¶

Load the synth1 - synth4 datasets into python using the loadmat function. The synthX data is a Matfile loaded into Python as a dictionary; the relevant data is contained under keys X and y.

Exercise 1.2¶

Cluster the data into K = 4 clusters using the k-means algorithm with the euclidian distance metric. Make a scatter plot of the data and the clustering using the provided clusterPlot() function from the toolbox. Move the legend if the position is obfuscating data.

Helpful hints:

  • Type clusterPlot(X,clusters,centroids,y) to plot the data and the clustering. Don't forget to import the function from the toolbox folder. If you are unsure about how to use the function, open the .py file in a text editor and take a look at documentation.
  • In Python, you can use the function KMeansClusterer() from the package nltk.cluster.kmeans to compute k-means clustering. please read the documentation of the function, as it creates an object which you can then use for clustering.
  • Use distance = nltk.cluster.util.euclidean_distance to use the euclidean distance metric!
In [19]:
## Answer to exercise 1.2
from toolbox import clusterPlot as cp
from nltk.cluster.kmeans import KMeansClusterer
from nltk.cluster.util import euclidean_distance
k1 = 4

def clustering(k, x, Y, metric):
#first we need to get clusters and centroids:
    clusterer = KMeansClusterer(k, metric, avoid_empty_clusters=True)
    clusters = clusterer.cluster(x, True)  #getting clusters from the clusterer
    centroids = clusterer.means()       #and getting the means AKA centroids from the clusterer

    #now we have everything we need for clusterPlot:
    cp.clusterPlot(x, clusters, centroids, Y)

clustering(k1, X1, y1, euclidean_distance)
In [12]:
clustering(k1, X2, y2, euclidean_distance)
In [4]:
clustering(k1, X3, y3, euclidean_distance)
In [13]:
clustering(k1, X4, y4, euclidean_distance)

Exercise 1.3¶

Does the clustering coincide with the true class? Explain for each of the four datasets.

ANSWER:

The clustering of the synth1 does coincide with the true class since from the clusterplot we can clearly see (and also from assignment 9) that we have 4 distinct clusters, which is also confirmed by the legend. All but one points are classified correctly.

The clustering of the synth2 does not concide well with the true class since from the clusterplot we can see that there are indeed 4 class labels but the clustering was unsuccessful (or very wrong). The clusters were also swayed by the outliers.

The clustering of synth3 does not concide well with the true class since from the clusterplot we can see that there are 4 class labels but the clustering was again unsuccessful. This happened because the objects aren't spherical. A DBSCAN would work well here.

The clustering of synth4 does not concide well with the true class since from the clusterplot we can see that the data is probably uncorrelated. So we're searching for a pattern that isn't there.

Evaluating how good your clustering is can be hard, because we don't always have labels. Generally, clustering is unsupervised. If we do however have labels, we can use the supervised measures of cluster validity described in Introduction to Data Mining section 8.5.7, in particular the entropy, purity, rand statistic, and Jaccard coefficient. Carefully review these measures in the book and make sure you understand how they are calculated.

#I want to revise making subplots so:
def kmeans_subplots(K):
    for x, y in [(X1, y1), (X2, y2), (X3, y3), (X4, y4)]:
        fig, axs = plt.subplots(5, 2, figsize=(8, 20))   #we have 10 plots for each dataset and we'll separate them into 5 rows of 2
        fig.suptitle("Dataset plots", fontsize=16)
        
        for idx, k in enumerate(range(1, K + 1)):
            ax = axs[idx // 2][idx % 2]     #picking position in the 5 x 2 grid
            plt.sca(ax)     #settinf the current axis
            clustering(k, x, y, euclidean_distance)
            
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    
    

kmeans_subplots(10)
In [34]:
def evaluation_of(K, metric):
    for x, y in [(X1, y1), (X2, y2), (X3, y3), (X4, y4)]:
        entropies  = []     #initiating all the evaluators
        purities   = []
        rands      = []
        jaccards   = []

        for k in range(1, K + 1):
            clusterer = KMeansClusterer(k, metric, avoid_empty_clusters=True)
            clusters = clusterer.cluster(x, True)

            entropy, purity, rand, jaccard = cv.clusterVal(y, clusters)     #calculating all validity measures

            entropies.append(entropy)
            purities.append(purity)
            rands.append(rand)
            jaccards.append(jaccard)

        #plotting
        plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
        ks = list(range(1, K + 1))

        plt.plot(ks, entropies, label="entropy")
        plt.plot(ks, purities, label="purity")
        plt.plot(ks, rands, label="rand index")
        plt.plot(ks, jaccards, label="jaccard")

        plt.xlabel("k")
        plt.ylabel("Cluster validity score")
        plt.title("Cluster validity for dataset")
        plt.legend()
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
    

evaluation_of(10, euclidean_distance)

Exercise 1.5¶

How can the cluster validity measures be used to select the best number of clusters? Does one of the datasets have a clear optimum?

What happens when more than four clusters are used to model the data? Explain for each dataset.

ANSWER:

Entropy can indicate the best number of clusters k by where the knee of the plot is. For the first dataset that would be either 2, 3 or 5. Purity generally increases as we increase the number of clusters. If the plot of purity agains k has some obvious "peaks" then we can try using that k as the number of clusters. Rand index works symmilarly. If we look at jaccard coefficient plotted against k, we can observe if we have any extreme maximum values. Those indicate the best choices for k determined by the jaccard. None of the k's in the clusters 2, 3 and 4 stand out as the best, but in dataset 1 we can observe that for K = 2, 3, 5 most of the measures indicate a good choice for k. This is interesting since you would think that there should be 4 clusters by looking at the plot of clusters. This just means that the measures only suggest good k's and don't produce the perfect one even if they all indicate one value for k.

After running the algorithm 2 more times the best value for k in the first dataset "changed" to 4. So by calculating the measures more than once we can get different results. If the results fluctuare a lot, the clustering is less stable.

Exercise 2.2¶

Cluster each dataset again, but use a different distance metric where you think it would help!

Helpful hints:

  • Use the implemented weighted_euclidean or nltk.cluster.util.cosine_distance as the distance
In [63]:
import numpy as np
from nltk.cluster.util import cosine_distance
weights = np.array([0.3,0.7])  # adjust as needed

def weighted_euclidean(u, v):
    u = np.asarray(u)
    v = np.asarray(v)
    return np.sqrt(((weights * (u - v)) ** 2).sum())
In [64]:
#first let's try the weighted euclidean:
evaluation_of(10, weighted_euclidean)
In [51]:
evaluation_of(10, cosine_distance)

Exercise 2.3¶

What are your final distance measures used for each cluster?

ANSWER:

for the first dataset, we can just use the normal euclidean distance we used in exercise 1, since it already told us which values to try for k.

For the second dataset, we can use the cosine metric since all of the measures tell us that a good choice for k is either 4 or 5, which is a close to optimal choice even though we cannot get the correct clustering from kmeans clustering.

For the third dataset, it's very hard to get a good k for the clustering. The weighted euclidean suggested k = 3 most times, which is close to the optimal value of clusters.

For the fourth dataset, all of the measures still differ and fluctuate a lot, meaning that we don't have a particulat pattern.

Exercise 4 - DBScan¶

In this part of the exercise we will investigate DBSCAN clustering. In DBSCAN, clusters are formed by identifying regions of high point density rather than assigning points to the nearest center. A point is considered a core point if it has enough neighboring points within a specified radius, and clusters are created by expanding outward from these core points to all other points that are reachable through dense regions. Points that do not belong to any such region are labeled as noise. Unlike k-means, DBSCAN does not iteratively update cluster centers, nor does it require the number of clusters to be specified in advance; instead, clustering finishes once all points have been visited and all dense regions have been fully expanded.

Exercise 4.1¶

For DBScan we are going to work with the moons dataset. This is a very common dataset in clustering. We will use several instances of this dataset, which you will generate yourself.

  • Use the make_moons function from sklearn.datasets to generate a dataset with 200 samples, with noise equal to 0.1.
  • Plot the dataset with the colour corresponding to the labels.
In [ ]:
## Answer to exercise 3.1
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
samples = 200

Xs, ys = make_moons(samples, noise=0.1)
cp.clusterPlot(Xs, ys)

Exercise 4.2¶

Use the DBSCAN function from sklearn.cluster to fit a clustering to the dataset you loaded above. Pick eps and min_samples such that you find a reasonable clustering. Describe if it is easy/hard/impossible to cluster the data perfectly.

In [ ]:
## Answer to exercise 3.2
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

clustering1 = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=4).fit(Xs)     #and getting the means AKA centroids from the clusterer
labels = clustering1.labels_

#now we have everything we need for clusterPlot:
cp.clusterPlot(Xs, labels, y=ys)
#cp.clusterPlot(Xs, clustering1, ys)

YOUR ANSWERS:

It is impossible to cluster the data perfectly because of noise, but if we remove it, we can cluster it pretty easily and almost perfectly. Maybe not the best but good enough parameters are Eps = 0.2 and MinPts = 4. When we choose these parameters only 2 points are clustered incorrectly. Point (0.25, 1.25) can easily be reassigned to the right class (which is the closest) if we say that there have to be exactly 2 clusters. The other point that is incorrectly classified could not be assigned to the right class, since the second and third closest points to it are from the wrong class. So for MinEps >= 3 it will always be assigned to the wrong one.

ANSWER:

If the noise is 0, the DBSCAN can always make a perfect observation (given enough points). We can use a lot of different Eps and MinPts and still get the perfect clustering.

When the sample size is small and we have too much noise, the data cannot be distinguished and properly clustered with DBSCAN.
